title: The loss of staff belonging in higher education
summary: Nick Hulbert-Williams argues that what looks like low morale and change fatigue in HE may really be a crisis of belonging
full_text:
As a practitioner-academic I often feel like I inhabit several different worlds at once.

What I love most about being the head of an academic department is that it allows me to bring those worlds together – drawing on my experience as a psychologist, coach, and academic leader to think about how we can better support staff and students in university settings.

It won’t be news to anyone that higher education is struggling. Here in the UK, we’ve seen unprecedented financial pressures, workforce shrinkage and organisational change on a scale that many of us have never experienced before. Some institutions are faring comparatively well against much of the sector, but even there, staff are still feeling the ripples of what’s happening elsewhere.

Like many colleagues in leadership positions, I often find myself holding two seemingly contradictory feelings at once. On one hand, I share the sense of sadness and uncertainty that these changes are creating across the sector. On the other, I find genuine challenge and purpose in helping to lead my team through the necessary process of adaptation, reorganisation and strategic change.

However much I may enjoy that leadership challenge, I can’t ignore what I am hearing from colleagues. Comments that once felt rare in academia – “I’ve checked out,” “I’m just doing what I need to get by,” “I’m keeping my head down” – now seem commonplace.

Making sense of the response

Recently, I attended the British Psychological Society Division of Coaching Psychology conference, where the theme was belonging.

Sitting in the audience, I realised that what I was observing across higher education wasn’t simply low morale or change fatigue.

The more I reflected on this, the more I realised that what we are witnessing may be a crisis of belonging. Belonging can be defined in many ways, but I particularly like Thissen et al.’s definition in which belonging reflects “…being valued, needed or important for others in a specific context and the feeling of fitting in through shared or complementary features.”

In psychology, belonging is generally understood to be a fundamental human need rather than a workplace luxury. Decades of research have shown that feeling accepted, valued and connected to others is closely linked to wellbeing, motivation and resilience. When belonging is disrupted, people don’t simply become less satisfied at work: they can begin to question their identity and place within a community.

Seen through that lens, many of the responses we are witnessing in staff across higher education suddenly make more sense.

Finding your tribe

I often talk to coaching clients and mentees about the importance of finding their tribe – a group of people, sometimes surprisingly small, with whom there is shared understanding, common purpose, and mutual trust. Tribes create that sense of individual belonging. They also provide psychological safety, creating spaces where ideas can be explored openly and where we can show up as our authentic selves.

You might imagine that authenticity would come naturally within universities. They are often viewed as intellectually curious and socially liberal environments. Yet I’m not sure that was ever entirely true. Academia has always been competitive. Expectations around performance and outputs can feel relentless. Challenging accepted wisdom or established ways of doing things is not always as comfortable as we might like to believe. It’s not a surprise that many working in academia feel a need to filter their authentic self in the workplace.

In that context, belonging does not happen by accident. It has to be actively created, nurtured and protected through thoughtful leadership and supportive communities.

Most of us belong to multiple tribes, but during the middle years of life our work tribe often becomes one of the most important because it is where we spend so much of our time and energy.

What concerns me is that many of those tribes are disintegrating around us, both physically and metaphorically.

The physical loss is perhaps the most obvious. Through restructuring, redundancy programmes and sector contraction, many of us have watched valued colleagues disappear from our day-to-day professional lives. Some move into different roles. Others leave institutions. Some leave higher education entirely.

The consequences extend beyond those who leave the sector. For those who remain, there is a quieter loss that often goes unrecognised. Years spent building trusted relationships, developing collaborations, creating shared projects and supporting one another can disappear remarkably quickly. The professional networks that took years to cultivate can fragment within months. We’re left with uncertainty and unease across many facets of our working world.

There is also a more subtle, metaphorical loss.

A different kind of loss

Compared to even a decade ago, academia simply feels different. Smaller workforces mean that many of us are being asked to do more with less. Research, scholarship and knowledge exchange activities are often squeezed by the demands of keeping core operations running. Beyond the obvious implications for universities and wider society, this shift may have important psychological consequences.

Psychologists have long recognised that our identities are shaped by the groups to which we belong. We do not simply think of ourselves as individuals; we understand ourselves through our membership of communities that matter to us.

For many academics, professional identity is not primarily tied to a particular institution. It is tied to being a psychologist, historian, engineer, biologist, or sociologist. It is forged through years of collaboration, conference attendance, mentorship and shared intellectual endeavour. It is built through specialist communities that provide meaning, purpose and belonging. When those communities begin to fragment, the loss is not merely practical. It can feel deeply personal.

Perhaps that is why so many colleagues seem lost, and as though their only means of survival is to “keep their heads down.” The challenge is not simply increased workload or uncertainty about the future. Many people are also navigating the loss of communities that helped define who they were professionally.

In some respects, what we are seeing resembles a form of collective grief. Not only grief for colleagues who have left, but grief for ways of working, professional identities and communities that once gave meaning to academic life. This creates an important challenge for university leaders.

There is no denying the scale of the task facing those in leadership positions. Financial sustainability matters. Organisational structures matter. Policies matter. Institutions cannot function without them. Yet these are fundamentally systems-level responses.

Coaching psychology makes excellent use of Self-Determination Theory to explain a range of workplace stressors. We know from this work that people are more likely to thrive when they experience competence, autonomy and meaningful connection with others. Universities have understandably invested enormous energy into redesigning structures and securing financial stability. But if belonging continues to erode, many staff will struggle to reconnect with the motivation and sense of purpose that drew them into academia in the first place. The challenge for leaders is, therefore, not simply to redesign organisations. It is to create the conditions in which communities can reform, and people can reconnect with a shared sense of purpose.

Belonging is not something that can be manufactured through a policy document or achieved through a single initiative. It requires time, investment, and genuine attention. It grows through relationships, trust, and shared endeavour. Academic leaders – myself included – need to recognise that something important has been lost. Alongside the difficult work of organisational change, we need to think much more creatively about how we help staff rebuild connection, rediscover purpose and find new tribes.

Because if we fail to do so, and somewhat urgently, I fear we will lose something far more significant than funding, structures, or organisational capacity. We risk losing the very communities that make academic life meaningful. And that is a loss from which the sector may struggle to recover.

title: When students turn to AI for wellbeing support, universities must rediscover how to be human

The post When students turn to AI for wellbeing support, universities must rediscover how to be human appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
For those attending this year’s party conferences, join HEPI for our 2026 Party Conference ringe events, at the Labour Party Conference on Monday 28 September in Liverpool and the Conservative Party Conference on Monday 5 October in Birmingham.

At both conferences, HEPI will host two events exploring some of the biggest issues facing higher education:

Higher Education Question Time, bringing together sector leaders to answer your questions about the key challenges and opportunities for universities,

Soft power in a hardening world: is the UK making the most of its global assets?, examining the UK’s international influence and the role of higher education within it.

All events take place outside the secure zones, so no conference pass is required. Register your interest now. As with all party conference fringe events, attendance is first come, first served and registering does not guarantee you will get a seat.

This blog was kindly authored by Dr Kieran Phelan, Assistant Professor in Human Geography, and School Senior Tutor at the University of Nottingham.

With the number of students with mental health conditions almost quadrupling over the last decade, the sector faces acute demand on its mental health support services. University mental health advisors report growing caseloads in both number and complexity, with over half considered ‘high risk’. Whilst student mental health remains a key institutional priority, efforts to improve capacity are often outpaced by demand, which is itself intensified by wider economic pressures. The cost of living crisis, housing insecurity, graduate labour market uncertainty and the challenge of balancing paid work alongside study compound existing risks associated with academic pressure, relocation and separation from established support networks.

We often imagine campus to be an enabler of good wellbeing – a place of rich social capital where community builds, friendships form and support is available to flourish and learn. However, increasingly, this imagination is outdated. Lecture halls are emptier, seminars are quieter, in-person engagement is lower and students report growing social isolation. Far from our social imagination of campus life, for growing numbers of students, life is defined through loneliness.

Some attribute this to wider societal shifts, including declining civic engagement and the growth of social media culture. Others have reflected on how campus itself shapes student experience, and how, intentionally or otherwise, it has become more asocial. The proliferation of online learning and lecture recordings, anonymous mass teaching and the decline of social third spaces have all weakened opportunities for connection and friendship building. Increasingly, the social ‘work’ traditionally associated with campus life can no longer be assumed.

This should concern anyone committed to student wellbeing. Students are simultaneously experiencing rising mental health pressures and growing barriers to support, whilst university services struggle to meet and resource escalating demand. When institutional support proves difficult to access, perhaps due to long waiting times or constrained working schedules, student support-seeking behaviours don’t disappear but are displaced into digital spaces outside of university support structures; on social media, online communities and across the internet more broadly.

Increasingly, AI-powered conversational platforms- chatbots- are becoming part of this landscape. Whilst concerns about ChatGPT-written essays continue to dominate institutional AI discussions, students are engaging with AI in far more varied and complex ways. So-called ‘pastoral AI’ is growing. Whilst mainstream tools such as Copilot and ChatGPT are designed for productivity, users are increasingly turning to them for life advice, wellbeing, and emotional support. Recent research suggests that therapy and companionship may now represent among the most popular AI use cases. The HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey found that around 15% of students are using AI for companionship, advice or to address loneliness

For students already experiencing poor mental health, the risks are especially acute. Conversations can amplify mania, validate psychosis and encourage unhealthy dependence rather than resolution. In the most troubling cases, chatbots have generated dangerous responses and encouraged harmful behaviour. Whilst extreme, such cases are products of sycophantic systems optimised for engagement, unbounded by therapeutic ethics and devoid of pastorally guided human intervention.

Why students are turning to AI for mental health and wellbeing support tells us a great deal about the student support ecosystem and what’s not working. Seventeen per cent of young people value AI because it is ‘always available’. Twelve per cent say they use chatbots because they have no one else to talk to, rising substantially amongst vulnerable young people, whilst ten per cent claim they would rather turn to AI than an adult for advice or wellbeing support. It speaks to the social worlds our young people are navigating, as well as how our campus and support environments appear to be failing to build, invest in and articulate the value of trusted and accessible human support infrastructures.

AI is already showing up in support and wellbeing services; the ambiguity of institutional AI policies, the threat of academic misconduct and the more general existential threats of AI, are already being discussed in support conversations. But rarely do we take seriously, on an institutional level, how AI is already being used beyond assessment by our students, and especially as a risky support replacements for our overstretched support and wellbeing services. This shift is just not yet institutionally acknowledged.

But with the growing use of pastoral AI and its known associated risks, higher education institutions urgently need to begin a different kind of AI conversation. This will require different voices of expertise; not just learning technologists or digital pedagogists, but also counsellors, pastoral advisers, and mental health professionals.

Yet, unlike academic misconduct policy, where levers of change are largely procedural, re-defining and re-shaping university support cultures will be more challenging and will demand a more expansive scope of effort and responsibility beyond the purview of support and wellbeing services alone. It will involve us all.

Sure, it might require rethinking student’s user experiences of existing support and wellbeing services, and might also require greater human resources to deliver more in-person and accessible support. This will no doubt be challenging given the sector’s stretched finances. But it will also demand that institutions elevate pastoral provision as part of a bigger mission-critical agenda of building better, more enabling, human-centred educational experiences, where their students are intentionally supported to build more enriching social capital together. Put simply, to build a campus that’s unapologetically human.

title: The Hidden Curriculum First-Gen Students Face
summary:
The Hidden Curriculum First-Gen Students Face
Joshua.Bay Thu, 09/10/2026 - 03:00 AM

In this week’s Voices of Student Success episode, University of Houston–Downtown’s Hope Pacheco discusses what first-gen students need to navigate college, find support and persist.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Being the first in your family to attend college can mean entering an unfamiliar system without the same knowledge or networks some of your peers have—from knowing where to turn for help to navigating financial aid, academics and the unwritten rules of campus life.

But first-generation students also bring their own experiences, strengths and support systems with them. So what do colleges still misunderstand about first-gen students—and what actually helps them feel like they belong and ultimately allow them to earn a degree?

Hope Pacheco, associate dean of students and executive director of the Gator Resource Center at the University of Houston–Downtown, joined Inside Higher Ed student success reporter Joshua Bay on Voices of Student Success to unpack what first-generation students experience when they arrive on campus, whom they turn to when they need help and what colleges can do to make sure they don’t have to figure it all out on their own.

Follow us on Apple Podcasts and Spotify

Here are five key takeaways on what colleges can do to better understand and support first-generation students.

First-gen students navigate a hidden curriculum.

For first-generation students, Pacheco said, navigating college can mean learning how a complicated set of deadlines, requirements and decisions fit together, often while they’re already expected to be making consequential choices about their education.

“There are a lot of things that I think that the academic calendar drives for students, especially first-gen students who are trying to figure out: Is this the right major for me? Is my financial aid award right? How much time do I have to drop a class or add a class?” Pacheco said.

“There’s information that’s shared through orientation and advising, and even precollege through their college counseling advisors,” she added. “The academic calendar can really drive some of the tensions that some of our first-gen students might feel about having to make decisions in the moment.”

Being first-gen shouldn’t be regarded as a deficit.

Pacheco said institutions often lump first-generation students together, but they aren’t a monolith.

“What I feel like we’re missing is the nuances of our traditional-age students, adult learners and older students who are coming back to complete a degree, and they can all be first-gen students as well,” Pacheco said. “[There are] nuances of what a first-generation college student experience is going to look [like] … across the age and the time that they’re coming to us.”

“What a first-gen traditional-age student might need is going to look different from [what] a parenting student working full-time or one who might be coming to us as a transfer student from community college [might need],” she added.

At the same time, Pacheco said, colleges shouldn’t define first-generation students only by the knowledge or experiences they may lack. Many are already advocates for their families and arrive on campus with skills they’ve developed while navigating other parts of their lives.

“The advocacy skills that [first-gen] students bring is important,” she said. “Even as we talk about students maybe not having the college knowledge, they’re coming to us with financial skills, they’re coming to us with skills that they’re having to not only blaze a trail to be the first, but also be a role model to their own family.”

Supporting first-gen students means supporting their families, too.

Pacheco said institutions often have an array of supports for students, but first-gen students still often lean on their families and communities, regardless of whether those people have firsthand college experience.

“We want to be there for students, but at the end of the day, it’s more than likely that they’re going to their family,” Pacheco said. “It's important when we are talking to families that they know that there is support at the university, and provide that information to families as early as possible.”

Giving families that information helps them understand that they don’t need firsthand experience with higher education to play an important role in helping their students navigate college, Pacheco said.

“This is your student, this is our student, this is our journey together,” Pacheco said. “Regardless of what type of education level they have or not, they are the experts of their students.”

Students need to establish trusting relationships before they will ask for help.

Pacheco said building trust with first-gen students starts with making it clear that they belong on campus—and then demonstrating that message through how institutions support them.

“What colleges can do is very simple: Say it out loud, say you belong here, put it on everything, write it everywhere,” Pacheco said. “We are institutionalizing ‘You belong here.’ We are walking the walk. We’re demonstrating that we value you and your experience. We value the nuanced experience of all of our students [and] see you as an individual.”

In practice, that means designing programming and supports around the first-gen experience, adjusting hours so students can utilize them when they need them most and, at its core, ensuring first-gen students are able to build meaningful relationships and connections with the campus community.

“We shouldn't assume that the student is going to trust us,” Pacheco said. “We have to actively build the relationship. Building is on us as faculty and staff to do the work, to do the lift. And if that means changing our hours, if that means doing the program three times instead of one, if that means moving it online, we do that.”

A sense of belonging can determine whether students stay.

Pacheco said she often asks first-gen students at her university what might prevent them from successfully completing the semester. Often, those conversations revolve around college affordability, financial aid, working while enrolled, or managing mental health challenges alongside their coursework.

“Students are coming in and they want to be able to get as much as they can in the shortest amount of time and work—they’re looking at a very straight path,” Pacheco said. “I try to encourage students to think about a winding road.”

“So maybe it’s affordability, maybe it’s basic needs, maybe there’s a crisis that’s happening with family or with themselves,” she added. “We want to be able to get them through a successful semester, but how can we do that and still preserve the student? Because at the end of the day, they’re human. They may have multiple priorities and time may not be on their side.”

Ultimately, Pacheco said, an institution that successfully cultivates an inclusive and welcoming environment for first-gen students ensures they know they won’t have to navigate those challenges alone.

“I want a student to feel like even if I don’t know, I can go to anybody and they can point me in a direction, and if I’m unsure, they’re going to walk with me,” Pacheco said.

“Walking with someone—literally—is what I think every first-gen student needs,” she added. “And can you walk with the people that they’re bringing with them? It might be their family, it might be their chosen family, it might be their community, their friends. Walking through all of the things to come, and eventually walking across that graduation stage.”

title: Preparing for a Changing College Athletics Landscape
summary:
Preparing for a Changing College Athletics Landscape
jessica.blake@… Thu, 09/10/2026 - 03:00 AM

Karen Weaver has been an elite athlete, a coach and a university athletics administrator. Her new book explores what college presidents—and fans—need to know to navigate the ever-shifting ecosystem of college sports.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
When Karen Weaver began her doctorate in higher education management at the University of Pennsylvania in 2007, she’d already spent over 30 years in college athletics—as a player, coach and athletic director. Still, there was a “disconnect” she said she couldn’t resolve.

“It didn’t matter what campus I was on, there was this anger at people who worked in athletics—as if athletics just had access to everything, and their priorities were higher than the academic or the student affairs priorities,” Weaver said. “So I took the doctoral degree to try to understand why.”

She found many of the answers in discussions with her classmates.

“I was so fortunate. My [Ph.D.] cohort of 24 had five sitting- or about-to-become-college presidents,” Weaver said. “And it was the conversations with them that gave me great insight, not only to what presidents assumed about college athletics, but also what athletics people were assuming the presidents understood.”

“That’s where I really began to see a gap that I’d be able to address.”

Now, almost 20 years later, college athletics programs face an unprecedented era of change. Athletes have more freedom than ever before, the cost of sports programs is skyrocketing and, in some cases, conferences are splitting at the seams. And yet, Weaver, who is now a professor at the University of Pennsylvania, says many of the same foundational challenges remain.

In her new book, Understanding College Athletics: What Campus Leaders Need to Know About College Sports, Weaver compiles the years of lessons she’s learned in the hopes of helping college presidents the way they helped her. By better connecting athletics and academics, she said, college presidents can create a strong foundation for informed decision-making and smart financing even when the future feels unpredictable.

Inside Higher Ed spoke with Weaver by phone about the book and the role presidents play in the ever-evolving landscape of college athletics.

The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: In the foreword, Michael Sorrell, a college president and former college athlete himself, says that this book is “badly needed by more than just college presidents.” So tell me, why is this book important now?

A: Too many times, we’ve selected presidents over the years without any regard to what they know or understand about college athletics. I talk about one case in the book where the only thing a potential president was asked in an interview was, “Can we beat our archrival this year?” That kind of isolationist way—not having to deal with athletics until you actually sit in the chair—has not been helpful to our institutions. So, I wanted to try to bridge that gap. As far as others outside of the president’s office, it’s important for the larger campus community to appreciate the nuances of college athletics. It’s easy to get mad at the spending that goes on within the department and think, “Well, why is that more important than academics?” But so much of why an institution says it wants people to embrace the athletic experience is about branding. It’s about reaching out to prospective students and their families, the earned and paid media that the university gets, the alumni engagement. We often talk about these things as if they’re automatics. But they are not. So understanding the ecosystem is important for a wide range of people.

Q: Throughout the book you talk about how little many college presidents know about athletics. Why is that when it is often such a big part of college and university life?

A: We’ve had a long history in higher education of isolating academics from athletics. They’ve been siloed for a variety of reasons. There might be a sense that it’s not as important as academics; it doesn’t impact our national rankings in the AAU. But I also think athletics has been operating in its own world, trying to focus on and be good at what it does.

To strengthen both sides of the equation, each has to understand the value that the other brings—especially in this era of great change in higher education and athletics. How can we make this work together, rather than operating in silos?

Q: Speaking of change, the book aims to answer three key questions: How do college athletics work? Why are they more than just an extracurricular these days? And how are they changing? I want to focus on that last one in particular. What changes do college presidents need to be paying the most attention to?

A: It’s the old assumptions. I can’t tell you how many alums I’ve talked to who say, “I want athletics to go back to the way it was. They were amateurs and they weren’t focused on getting paid.” These alumni are becoming disenchanted with the new world of college athletics.

We need to help them understand that it is not going back because of the issues surrounding the antitrust violations. Athletes deserve to get a portion of the money that was generated, particularly at the bigger schools. We know things are not going to go backwards. But we don’t know what the new organizational structure is going to look like. So we can’t assume that our [current students, who will become alumni] are always going to be in our court and willing donors to our program. They consume sports differently. They come to games late. They leave early. All of those things have changed so much. So we have to really check our assumptions.

We also have to accept the fact that the budgets are changing dramatically. So, we have to ask, what can we afford to do? And we have to be realistic about the costs involved, including paying people and staffing things correctly, like athletic medicine, academic advisers, those types of things. It’s just not a head coach who’s going to go out and recruit. That’s where things were, you know, 15 or 20 years ago.

Presidents are just becoming aware of where the money comes from to fund the budgets.

Many presidents come to a campus where maybe 50 or 60 percent of the athletics budget is funded by the university tuition and student fees—and they’re probably surprised about that. And that’s just talking about Division I, because in Division II and Division III, almost all the budget is subsidized by tuition and fees.

When you really look at that funding model in this era of rising tuition costs, growing student fees and the pushback from students who don’t want their fees to go to funding athletic revenue share, presidents realize it’s a whole different context. The easy answer would be to say, “Fine, athletics, if you want to have revenue share, then you’ve got to go outside and look for it.” But presidents are realizing they must have a better understanding.

Q: Can you say more about NIL and revenue sharing and what presidents need to know in those areas?

A: It was always kind of crazy that everybody else on campus—whether they were working in the cafeteria or the president—could monetize their name, image and likeness because it’s an inherent right. Yet the athletes couldn’t. So, now that’s one of the greatest advances for athletes, but it’s been a real shock to the general public. And it comes with a side issue of mental health. The market is exploding for certain athletes, but other athletes are really struggling with the mental health challenges of trying to always promote themselves and brand themselves and get more followers and likes on their social media. So schools have really got to address the pressure that athletes are putting on themselves.

In the revenue-share area, we can talk about football and men’s basketball, but we have underresourced other sports, particularly women’s sports, in terms of promoting them, working to get them on TV … So leaders need to be thinking about the fact that we’ve been undervaluing other sports for so long. You look at the growth in not only women’s basketball but in softball and volleyball and other sports that are emerging, and there’s a whole explosion that we just have not accounted for. It could be a real upside, but it also creates competition for attention and time and all those kinds of things.

Q: So considering all of that, what do college leaders need to know to lead well?

A: Well, I’ve asked myself that question over the years, and the one thing that I try to emphasize throughout the book is [that they have to ask]: What is our mission? How does athletics relate to our mission as we are today, not to how we were 20 or 30 years ago? We know how much the landscape has changed on both sides [academics and athletics]. So, to assume that what we’ve always done is what we’re going to do in the future is not right for either side.

Q: What do you make of the recent dustup between Louisiana State University and the Southeastern Conference over whether athletes who have played professionally can play on a college team? How does it relate to the arguments in your book?

A: Fundamentally, what we’re wrestling with is who’s in charge and who has the authority to crack down and say you’re not following our guidelines.

Being a member of a conference is a privilege. It’s not a right. And while we haven’t seen a lot of instances of schools being kicked out of conferences, we can look to other examples like the Pac-12’s near implosion as an example of what happens when you do break things up. It becomes a different landscape financially.

So conferences are a little hesitant to blow things up, but they’re also very hesitant to have a school in there that doesn’t feel like they’re following the rules.

You also have to understand the structure of a conference. Presidents make up the board. So ultimately, while they are supposed to put the conference first, there’s this inherent tension. Often, presidents are caught saying, “I’m supposed to operate on behalf of my institution. That’s my job here.”

So this really puts presidents right in the middle. I don’t think we’ve really talked about that enough.

Q: On that note, Sorrell also noted in the foreword that “athletics at every level are out of control.” Do you agree with that? And if so, can you help me understand how we got there and why it’s important for college presidents and others to acknowledge that level of mayhem before they move forward and try to address the college athletics system?

A: Do you have an hour?

I would say that at some institutions that may be true because they’ve just allowed spending to continue, and they’ve assumed that they can always raise enough money. But for the vast majority of institutions, it’s been these sudden shifts in the legal landscape—whether it’s about revenue sharing, restrictions on noncash compensation or changes to transfer options—that have forced them to ask: What does this mean for us?

For example, when your rosters are changing every year—if not every semester—you don’t have that consistency. So the assumptions we’ve made about enrollment and retention, recruiting, and the ability to sell a four-year degree are all unsettled right now.

For presidents who want stability, that is really a very difficult place to be.

And secondly, I would say—and this is probably different than what you’re expecting—we have pressure coming from underneath in the youth sports area.

That’s because youth sports are exploding with private equity money, so they’re building fancy new facilities and they’re paying for travel teams. The average cost per year is now $10,000 per youth sports participant in order for them to play in the travel ball leagues.

If they come to college and don’t see that kind of experience, why would they choose your school over somewhere else? So that bottom-up pressure coming from youth sports is real, and that could really impact the university athletic programs’ recruitment and retention.

Q: What role, if any, do you think Congress should play in setting the rules and guiding colleges to address the out-of-control system?

A: I think fundamentally we have to make the changes ourselves. I don’t think we can look to Congress to solve it, because as many people know, when you look to Congress you get some of what you want, but you get much of what you don’t want. And that can be really problematic for college athletics.

We’re often looking for someone else to solve our problems, and I really believe we [as higher ed institutions] have to solve many of our problems ourselves.

Q: What do you think people—including college presidents and the broader public—should watch out for over the next few years when it comes to college athletics?

A: My hope is that people—including the media [and] alumni—would be respectful of the realities that university leaders are facing when they make difficult decisions.

They could be about a whole host of things like adding and dropping programs, changing divisions, etc. That’s a very real possibility for a number of schools, because they just can’t afford where they are. And while it’s really easy to be critical of a school that leaves one conference to be more competitive in another, that’s the reality of this situation right now.

No. 2, I’d like to see us get back to emphasizing the value of our degrees; they carry more than just revenue generation. What we can offer is lifetime earnings for so many of these athletes. This may be a moment in time when they make money, but what happens next?

In this era of revenue sharing and NIL, many presidents have accepted that they’re not going to be the only stop in an athlete’s academic journey. But they also need to be focused on creating a positive experience while they’re at their school and say, “We’re not just going to throw in the towel. We’re going to do what we can to make this young man or woman a stronger candidate for jobs when they graduate.”

Q: Are college athletics fixable? And if so, what will it take to reach the solution?

A: I believe that they are fixable, but I think we truly have to separate ourselves out from trying to be semipro.

And if that means a group of colleges have got to go off and do that by themselves, and everybody else looks at a different model—possibly a model that’s more educationally focused than championship-only focused—that might be the way to go.

title: How Some Colleges Responded to DOD’s Foreign Partnerships Order
summary:
How Some Colleges Responded to DOD’s Foreign Partnerships Order
Katherine Knott Thu, 09/10/2026 - 03:00 AM

To maintain eligibility for research funding, the Defense Department asked 30 universities to conduct an audit and report their findings by Aug. 31. All 30 responded, the department says.

Byline(s)
Katherine Knott
full_text:
The Trump administration’s decision to expand the number of foreign academic and research institutions that are considered off-limits for research partnerships has ended at least one study abroad program and triggered reviews at more than two dozen universities.

The Department of Defense can’t use “any funds for fundamental research that involves collaboration” with the entities included on what’s known as the Section 1286 list, which identifies institutions “confirmed to be engaging in activities that threaten U.S. national security interests,” according to the agency. That ban also extends to colleges that receive federal funding, according to DOD, and failure to comply could threaten that money.

After updating the Section 1286 list in July and adding several major research universities in China, DOD told 30 colleges to review their partnerships with institutions on the list and terminate any “problematic” relationships. Currently, 130 academic and research institutions located in China, Iran and Russia are off-limits for collaboration.

DOD said in an Aug. 17 news release that the audit request went to colleges and universities with active ties and collaborations with foreign entities on the list, “as well as organizations associated with rebranded Confucius Institutes.”

To maintain eligibility for research funding, the universities had to conduct the audit and report their findings by Aug. 31. The department told Inside Higher Ed last week that all 30 responded; officials are reviewing the responses “to ensure compliance with strengthened research security standards.”

Department officials have said the review “is designed to protect American taxpayer-funded research investments from unauthorized technology transfer, intellectual property theft and adversarial exploitation.”

The American Federation of Teachers and the American Association of University Professors condemned the directive in a statement last month, arguing it places the universities under suspicion and bypasses due process. “It remains unclear what legal authority permits the Department of War to condition all federal research funding, rather than just its own budget, on compliance with this order,” the unions said, using the Trump administration’s preferred name for the agency.

Inside Higher Ed reached out to all 30 U.S. institutions to learn more about what they told the department; nine responded and only a few of those shared their letters to DOD. The responses indicate that while the department’s directive focused on research activities, other types of academic partnerships with institutions in China could face more scrutiny.

The University of North Carolina told DOD that it ended a study abroad program with Fudan University in China “out of an abundance of caution.” The university’s compliance software flagged the program in late July after the updated Section 1286 list was released.

UNC’s review also identified two unfunded research projects with two institutions on the list. Neither project involves federal funding or access to UNC’s campus. Still, the faculty involved agreed to end the projects after they publish the results of the research.

A University of Minnesota spokesperson said that its review didn’t identify “any current activities that constitute specific research collaborations or arrangements of national security concern.” However, the university is evaluating a handful of “active academic exchange programs” identified in the review; the goal is to wind them down “appropriately,” the spokesperson said.

At a few universities, DOD identified a specific partnership or program that no longer exists.

The University of South Carolina ended its dual-degree business program with Shanghai Jiao Tong University in February “in response to evolving federal research security requirements and risk considerations,” according to the university’s Aug. 17 response to the department. A Bryant University spokesperson said its accounting program with Beijing Institute of Technology Zhuhai ended in 2024.

The spokesperson added the program “did not include any research activities” or “any collaboration on federally funded research projects.”

Several universities declined to share what they sent to DOD, though they acknowledged their responsibility to protect U.S. research and comply with federal laws.

Others said they are continuing with their partnerships.

Northeastern State University in Oklahoma told KTUL in Tulsa that it reviewed its relationship with Guangzhou College of Technology and Business and identified no research security risk. “The review confirmed that the relationship with GCTB is limited exclusively to undergraduate teaching and degree completion,” the statement said.

Drake University President Marty Martin said in a campus message that DOD requested that Drake review its ties with Qingdao University as an institution located in a foreign country of concern, according to Drake’s student newspaper, The Times-Delphic. Qingdao is not on the Section 1286 list, and Martin said he didn’t “foresee any impact” to the partnership, which includes a dual-degree program.

“Complexity is something a globally engaged university builds the capacity to manage—it is not a reason to retreat from the work,” Martin wrote. “We remain deeply committed to our mission of preparing students for responsible global citizenship.”

title: Trump Admin. Says UC Berkeley Law, Duke Med School Discriminated in Admissions
summary:
Trump Admin. Says UC Berkeley Law, Duke Med School Discriminated in Admissions
Johanna Alonso Thu, 09/10/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
The Departments of Justice and Health and Human Services announced this week that they had determined the University of California, Berkeley’s law school and Duke University’s medical school each intentionally discriminated against white and Asian applicants in their admissions practices. The DOJ and the Department of Education jointly investigated Berkeley, while HHS investigated Duke.

The investigations are the Trump administration’s sixth and seventh findings of admissions discrimination, including findings released last month about Duke’s law school. So far, the administration has launched at least 29 investigations into admissions practices at universities. Twenty-seven of those investigations are looking into medical school admissions, and 15 of the medical schools being investigated have not yet been named.

As with previous medical school investigations, HHS’s letter to Duke pointed out that the average MCAT scores of admitted Black and Hispanic students were lower than the average scores of admitted white and Asian students, noting that Black and Hispanic applicants were both admitted at higher rates than their white and Asian counterparts.

Department officials also argued that the institution intended to discriminate, based on internal communications in which administrators discussed how to maintain student diversity following the Supreme Court’s 2023 ban on affirmative action in admissions. Those strategies included considering minority applicants’ discussions of challenges they’d faced in their essays, which Chief Justice John Roberts said was acceptable in the ruling.

The findings of discrimination at Berkeley’s law school rely on the same central arguments. The DOJ’s letter to Berkeley uses Berkeley Law Dean Erwin Chemerinsky’s public support of affirmative action in interviews, opinion articles and university materials as evidence that Berkeley intentionally discriminated. The DOJ also notes places in the Berkeley Law application where students are encouraged to discuss their race.

The LSAT scores of students admitted to the law school also differed by race, according to the DOJ; among the combined 2024 and 2025 incoming classes, half of admitted Black students had scores that were lower than the scores of 95 percent of admitted white students

Some civil rights experts have criticized the Trump administration’s admissions investigations for not being thorough enough and relying too heavily on statistical evidence. In the letter to Duke’s medical school, the HHS Office for Civil Rights noted that it offered the university an opportunity to explain the gaps in MCAT scores, but that officials had “failed to respond” to that inquiry.

“OCR found that Duke School of Medicine intentionally discriminates against applicants by granting and denying admission based on an applicant’s race, breaking federal anti-discrimination laws. In the Trump Administration, we are committed to ensuring that every applicant at a medical school is treated equally. Any kind of discrimination through the admissions process is unacceptable,” said Paula M. Stannard, director of the HHS Office for Civil Rights, in the department’s announcement.

The Duke School of Medicine investigation is the first of its kind to be completed by HHS; the Departments of Justice and Education have conducted the other 27. In its announcement, HHS noted that it has given the university almost $3.5 billion in funds over the past five years.

In a statement, a Duke spokesperson said the university is reviewing HHS’s letter. “Duke is committed to complying with the law and will continue to do so in a manner that is consistent with our academic mission,” they added.

title: Youth losing critical skills and AI 'hollowing out' capabilities, PISA founder says
summary: The father of the world-famous standardised PISA tests warned that a dramatic decline in parental interest and tech-driven behavioural changes could be behind record-low student performances.
full_text:
The picture of student performance in Europe is "really concerning", with a recent report showing young people are losing essential skills that are "particularly important for the times we live in", Andreas Schleicher, the founder of the OECD's renowned PISA tests, has told Euronews.

The results of the 2025 standardised test, taken by 15-year-olds across 91 countries, were released this week, and found that performance in reading and mathematics had reached record lows across OECD countries.

The assessment measures students’ ability to apply reading, mathematics and science skills to real-world problems.

"We see that young people not only have lower literacy skills, but we are seeing a decline in students' capacity to triangulate and to critically reflect on information, to engage with more complex texts," said Schleicher, adding that these are essential skills in the world of artificial intelligence (AI).

"This technology is not necessarily accurate and therefore that intuition to check and verify should be really present," he added.

He also described a vicious cycle in which young people's use of such tools, which "are not designed to make us think harder", is further "hollowing out exactly the capabilities that we need". This was reflected in the PISA results: Students not using AI tend to be higher-performing.

"The bottom line is quite simple: You don't get fit by watching sports. You get fit by doing sports," Schleicher said. "And the same is true with learning. Learning doesn't come through the consumption of content; learning comes by engaging with ideas to compare and contrast. And AI can hollow out that very process. That's what we observe."

One factor at play is that the speed at which new technologies such as AI have advanced in many countries outpaces education systems' ability to reform. "Humans have always been better at inventing new things than using them wisely," Schleicher said.

However, the OECD assessment also found that guided, active use that forces cognitive friction — for example, challenging AI's output — translates to better learning outcomes.

"There are really interesting examples of countries where AI is used to make pupils think harder, to make them think about the right questions, to give teachers powerful tools to help students learn better," Schleicher said, adding that the education system needs to "shift gears away from a consumptive use of AI to a more creative use."

Small countries stand out

Schleicher has become one of the most influential voices in global education since he created the PISA test during the 1990s.

"We started work on this because, in the 90s, we measured success in education mainly by how much was spent on education and for how many years pupils sat in a classroom, which actually tells us very little" about the skills produced, he explained.

The assessments provide data-driven comparisons of national education systems across the world, and highlight major discrepancies, even within Europe. The latest results show that pupils' scores in seven EU countries were significantly above the OECD average, while in 13 member states, they were considerably below it.

"The biggest declines were recorded in large European countries, like France, Germany, and Spain. The most interesting solutions were found in the small, dynamic economies," Schleicher said.

An example is Estonia: Its students ranked first in Europe and in the global top ten in all three domains of the assessment. "It's a clear example of a country that is engaging with the digital world in a cautious but very thoughtful, very productive way," Schleicher explained.

Advice for parents and teachers

When looking to the future, Schleicher stressed that the focus should shift away from teaching skills that are easy to digitise, to more human skills such as "ethical decisions" and "our capacity to navigate complex human relationships".

He noted that students can no longer be "passive consumers" of education, but should become active learners. This raises questions in many parents' minds after the test results came out: What can they do?

"For parents, the answer is really simple. One of my real concerns is that parental interest in education in Europe has dramatically declined."

He explained that the solution is less about "doing three hours of homework with your child at the kitchen table" and more about "showing your child that what they are working on in school really matters to you".

Children whose parents ask them how their school day went, he noted, are two school years ahead in their test results.

Meanwhile, teachers' job should expand from being a good instructor to being "a great coach, a good mentor, a great facilitator" who takes a "genuine interest in who your students are and who they want to become and to accompany them on that journey".

However, in a Europe where many countries are suffering from teacher shortages, he stressed that the education system must "give teachers more time and more to play that much more important role."

title: 42% students express interest in continuing studies into fourth year under Keralam’s FYUGP: survey
summary: A total of 66,014 students presently pursuing their third year of undergraduate studies participated in the survey by Kerala State Higher Education Council. Students from all universities that have implemented FYUGP participated
full_text:
Around 42% of students enrolled in Keralam’s first batch of the Four-Year Undergraduate Programme (FYUGP) have expressed interest in continuing their studies into the fourth year, according to a State-level survey conducted by the Kerala State Higher Education Council (KSHEC).

A total of 66,014 students presently pursuing their third year of undergraduate studies participated in the survey. Students from all universities in Keralam that have implemented the FYUGP participated in the survey.

When asked about their plans after completing the third year, 23,951 students said they intended to continue into the fourth year of the FYUGP. Another 5,468 students said they planned to join two-year postgraduate programmes after completing the third year. A total of 7,123 students expressed an intention to seek employment, while 3,574 said they planned to prepare for competitive examinations.

Notably, 2,148 students expressed interest in pursuing higher studies outside Keralam and 1,388 indicated a preference for higher studies abroad. As many as 20,752 students said they had not yet reached a final decision regarding their future studies. Only 162 students expressed interest in opting for the N-1 pathway, which enables students to fast-track their studies and graduate ahead of schedule.

The survey also sought to ascertain the level of certainty among students about continuing into the fourth year. As many as 13,912 students said they would “definitely” continue, while 12,865 said they would “most probably” continue.

Regarding the choice of study pathway in the fourth year, 12,780 students expressed a preference for the Honours programme, while 11,653 preferred Honours with Research. Another 8,903 students said they would choose either pathway depending on the opportunities available to them. Taken together, 33,336 students expressed interest in the Honours or Honours with Research pathways.

At the same time, the survey highlighted a significant demand for greater academic guidance before students make decisions about their future study and career paths. As many as 20,181 students said they needed more academic guidance before making a final decision.

The finding points to a substantial requirement for clearer information and counselling on the fourth-year study options, research opportunities, postgraduate education, employment prospects and skill-development pathways, official sources said.

The survey included questions on where students would prefer to pursue their fourth year, whether those exiting after the third year intended to immediately join a two-year postgraduate programme, the types of postgraduate programmes they preferred, their understanding of the various academic pathways available after the third year and the academic areas in which they required greater guidance.

A senior official pointed out that universities and colleges could play a key role by offering students comprehensive information on the Honours and Honours with Research options, available subjects, research facilities and opportunities for further study and employment. Such orientation would help students make more informed choices about their academic futures.

title: EC English halts new student arrivals worldwide this weekend
summary:
EC English Language Centres has said it will not be able to accept students due to arrive at its worldwide schools this weekend.

The post EC English halts new student arrivals worldwide this weekend appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
In correspondence with agents seen by The PIE News, EC English said: “due to unforeseen operational circumstances, we are unable to accept any new student arrivals to our EC English schools this weekend”.

The school said it would not be able to provide students with their planned program or accommodation and asked agents to contact students immediately to tell them the news.

“We appreciate that this is extremely short notice and that this will be particularly difficult for you, your students and their families who have put trust in you as their booking agent, especially where flights and other travel arrangements have already been made.”

“We are deeply sorry for the disruption and uncertainty this will undoubtably cause.”

EC English said its immediate priority was to ensure that students due to travel this weekend did not commence their journeys, and that it would provide an update to partners “when the position has been confirmed”.

The company did not immediately respond to The PIE’s request for comment.

We are unable to accept any new student arrivals to our EC English schools this weekend

EC English Language Centres

Established in 1991, EC English runs 25 language schools across the US, UK, Canada, Ireland, Malta, South Africa and Dubai. Its students come from over 120 countries.

The company closed its Bristol school this June and is set to close its Montreal site at the end of September, after a strategic review of its global operations earlier this year.

With plans to launch new summer programs in Spain and China, it said that closing the sites would allow it to direct more resources towards its strongest-performing centres.

“By focusing our investment on fewer locations, we are positioning EC to deliver even greater quality and impact in the years ahead.” EC English CEO Andrew Mangion told The PIE at the time.

The PIE understands that the shock news of its inability to accept students this term has caused panic among education agents globally.

It follows two consecutive years of decline for English Language Teaching (ELT) globally, with new data revealing student weeks fell by 23% in 2025, while student numbers dropped by 10%.

With experts forecasting further drops in 2026, they have warned providers to adapt to the emergence of a new market structure with fewer adult learners, shorter stays, and more opportunities in the juniors market.

title: US edtech nonprofit Technovation named PIEoneer of the year
summary:
Technovation was recognised at The PIEoneer Awards 2026 for helping underrepresented young people develop technology-based solutions to challenges in their communities.

The post US edtech nonprofit Technovation named PIEoneer of the year appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
US-based technology education nonprofit Technovation has won the flagship PIEoneer of the year award for its work supporting underrepresented young people to become technology innovators and problem-solvers.

The award was presented during the 10th anniversary of The PIEoneer Awards at London’s Guildhall, where winners across 21 categories were recognised for their contributions to international education.

“Receiving the PIEoneer of the year award is an honor for Technovation,” said founder Tara Chklovski.

“The PIEoneer of the year award is a reminder that the work we do transcends our organisation’s community, and equipping youth with proper educational tools is society’s best path forward.”

Chklovski, who founded Technovation 20 years ago to help girls develop the skills to shape their futures, said the recognition reflected the work of its more than 500,000 alumni worldwide and their challenge to limits imposed on them by society.

Technovation combines project-based learning with mentorship and a global competition in which students identify local challenges before developing technology-based solutions to address them. Its programmes cover areas including artificial intelligence, coding, entrepreneurship and leadership.

Founded in 2006 under the name Iridescent, Technovation began by organising family science events in Los Angeles. It has since developed into a global nonprofit supported by volunteer mentors, parents and local communities.

The PIEoneer of the year award is a reminder that the work we do transcends our organisation’s community, and equipping youth with proper educational tools is society’s best path forward

Tara Chklovski, Technovation

Technovation Girls, one of its core programmes, supports girls working in teams to design and code mobile applications responding to problems they have identified around them. Participants receive guidance from mentors as they turn their ideas into working products and present them through an international competition.

Former participants have gone on to enter startup and app-building competitions, speak at events including TEDx Women and IBM India Onward, and participate in the Google Science Fair. Some have also secured internships with technology companies, universities and government agencies.

Technovation was selected from a shortlist featuring organisations and initiatives working across global education, professional development, family mobility and post-conflict recovery.

Other finalists included Boundless Life, which provides education centres, furnished homes, coworking facilities and community support for internationally mobile families across eight countries.

The Netherlands-based GlocalShift Foundation was shortlisted for its Return to Rebuild Scholarship Programme for Gazans. The initiative has raised $650,000 with its partners to support hundreds of medical students, with its first graduates preparing to return and contribute to rebuilding Gaza’s healthcare system.

NAFSA, Common Purpose and Times Higher Education were recognised for the International Education Professional Certificate, which has enrolled 289 participants from 92 universities and organisations across 15 countries.

The Forum on Education Abroad was shortlisted for its Career Catalyst campaign, launched in 2025 to examine the professional and economic benefits of studying abroad. Its research found that business school students who studied overseas earned a $4,159 salary premium in their first jobs after graduation.

The remaining finalists were UK-based The JADE App and India’s The Outreach Collective, with the latter also receiving the highly commended recognition.

title: Productive Friction: What Universities Must Protect in the Age of AI
summary:
One of the readings that my students always pick as their favorite lesson about digital media economics comes from the late 1990s when Google engineers accidentally found gold in their trash. When they launched their search engine, it was working perfectly and millions of users were using it every day. Their algorithm was elegant and the results […]

The post Productive Friction: What Universities Must Protect in the Age of AI appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
One of the readings that my students always pick as their favorite lesson about digital media economics comes from the late 1990s when Google engineers accidentally found gold in their trash. When they launched their search engine, it was working perfectly and millions of users were using it every day. Their algorithm was elegant and the results outperformed other competitors in the market. However, their major problem was that no one had figured out how to make profit from the search. A few years later, they discovered that every search query that users typed left behind a trail of behavioral signals. Not only did the search tag the topic users typed in but it showed what they were searching for, how they phrased it, what they clicked on, what they ignored and how long they lingered. In the early years, this data was largely seen as the exhaust of the search engine, and it was essentially discarded as waste. But when the engineers aggregated all of this discarded behavioral data, it revealed things about people’s true desire and intent. So, Google could suddenly sell not just the demographics of their customers to advertisers but also the implied aspirations of all of their search queries.

This story I teach in my media criticism course comes from Shoshana Zuboff’s book “The Age of Surveillance Capitalism.” Zuboff explains that the most valuable asset of the search engine was always the “exhaust fumes” and for the longest time they were hidden in plain sight. Once Google realized that the byproduct of the search process was the thing they could monetize, it propelled the company to become the largest seller of digital advertising in the world.

Currently, higher education might be going through a similar moment. AI has now become a part of everyday life on college campuses and I have embraced it in all my classes at every level. I now encourage my students to use NotebookLM when the text becomes dense or incomprehensible. I encourage the students to upload assigned text to create timelines, flashcards for studying and video summaries of their reading. Students can now process text faster, research more effectively and edit their work without having to go to the writing center. These gains are substantial and any serious conversation about AI in education must begin with acknowledging the benefits of AI.

When Making Learning Easier Makes it Harder

However, there is a counterintuitive aspect to the AI-assisted learning that resembles the situation from the Google’s experience with “digital exhaust.” Just as Google almost discarded its most valuable byproduct, universities now risk bypassing the very thing that makes learning stick. The cognitive effort involved in learning and writing that we willingly outsource to AI may turn out to be the part that matters most. The energy needed to work through a difficult text, the discomfort of holding conflicting ideas in working memory, the pressure of constantly reorganizing one’s own thought process all seem like efforts we are glad to hand over to AI. But these experiences, what psychologist Paul Bloom and his colleagues call friction, are not incidental to learning. They suggest that friction may be the primary mechanism by which learning transforms the human mind. At present, AI is helping to remove this cognitive struggle from the thinking process, treating it as the exhaust of learning.

So now, realizing that friction could be useful, I have to face the dilemma that my use of our campus-approved Copilot AI may be helping students in the short term but hurting them in the long term. Could my encouragement of artificial intelligence as a brainstorming partner, summarizer and comprehension assistant produce net-negative results?

It’s no surprise that people outside of academia have noticed this problem already. Journalist Ezra Klein, a rather enthusiastic user of AI, mentioned earlier this year that the knowledge AI provides for him doesn’t change him in the same way reading does. He says that AI informs him without significant transformation. He ponders the value of the struggle that the demanding encounter with a difficult problem has on people experiencing it. In other words, the struggle is not a sign of faulty process, instead it is the very mechanism by which meaningful learning happens.

I’ve seen this in my classroom when students who have used AI to summarize a reading can identify its main argument, but by the time the discussion progresses beyond the basics, they have little to work with because they haven’t thought it through. The knowledge is there but it did not transform thinking, it just helped with comprehension.

Not All Friction is Created Equal

Psychologists Emily Zohar, Paul Bloom, and Michael Inclicht make a similar argument in a 2026 paper called “Against Frictionless Artificial Intelligence.” They point out two kinds of friction: excess and productive friction. Throughout history, humans invented technology in order to eliminate excess frictions which made life difficult and unproductive. The washing machine is an example of such a tool and today nobody looks back on washing clothes in the river with nostalgia. Productive friction, on the other hand, is the kind of effort that is the basis of real progress and meaningful growth. When we work through a hard problem without knowing the answer and sit in the discomfort of ambiguity, the pressure of thinking benefits us in the long run. Removing it damages the condition under which real learning occurs.

We might currently be approaching education’s digital exhaust moment. The productive friction generated by genuine intellectual struggle could be the very byproduct of the learning process that we might not want to get rid of that easily. The story of Google’s engineers who were too focused on the search to notice the exhaust offers an invaluable lesson. Consequently, the launch of AI into the university classroom serves as opportunity to ask the harder question: What does learning look like in a future that has automated the hardest parts of thinking?

The answer to the question should combine the right amount caution and innovation. When Google discovered the value of its exhaust, it packaged it deliberately, built infrastructure around it, and made it the centerpiece of their new business model. Universities now have same opportunity and should be highly motivated to do something equivalent. Refusing to use AI at this point is as futile and misguided as it was when professors were forbidding students to use the Internet in the 1990s. Recognizing that cognitive friction is the exhaust of the learning process, and building deliberately around is best lesson that can be drawn grom Google’s experience. Teaching students to protect and exercise productive friction should become one of the major pedagogical goals of the university of the future, and the following are three concrete strategies worth taking seriously.

Make Deep-Reading a Learning Goal

Deep-reading or slow and analytical examination of a text has been a proven pedagogical strategy that trains much needed attention and patience through which the human mind develops and transforms. The first task is to reintroduce it as essential practice of analytical thinking beyond basic English or composition classes. Walter J. Ong, who wrote about reading and writing as transformative technologies, suggested that reading throws the psyche back on itself and this introspection is what AI bypasses when it summarizes or ‘reads’ for us. Building structured, deep-reading exercises into introductory-level seminars would allow students to relearn how to pay attention to slow and focused engagement with long texts. In turn, we should change the assessments so that they can reward the quality of a student’s encounter with a text rather than the polish writing at the end of semester. NotebookLM may be used with difficult texts, but intentional exercises in deep reading should become a learning objective in many more courses at all levels. In my own courses, I have purposefully reinserted the encounter with the text as one of the main pedagogical goals of the course, pausing to read with students in class and teaching them to develop reading maps and timelines before moving toward more complex research.

Build Productive Friction Into Argumentation

Furthermore, the Hegelian dialectic should be taught as an explicit form of critical thinking and not as an implied philosophical aspiration. I have been a teacher for three decades and one of the most reliable ways to communicate critical thinking to my students has been through the practice of dialectical thinking. Put simply, for every thesis, students must develop an antithesis. Both must be considered with care before they can be reconciled through synthesis. Students can now easily ask the AI to produce a synthesis without any awareness or effort of what it takes to create such complexly integrated logic. Dialectical thinking should become a part of any argumentation-building assignment; the work should always show the thesis and its genuinely developed opposite. Only after the student has endured the tension of opposing thoughts, should they be permitted to find a way to reconcile those. There are undoubtedly classes that already require students to construct the most persuasive version of the argument through synthesis, but this might be the time to an opportunity to demand that AI help build this essential competency. In these scenarios, AI can generate counterarguments to which students must respond. Students could be encouraged to play a ‘devil’s advocate’ to the arguments built by AI. Or AI can provide models of synthesis itself. But in my classes, I always insist that the synthesis not be rushed, that students learn to embrace the discomfort of holding opposing ideas, and that the effortful navigation of conflicting tension is worth more than a comfortable conclusion.

Give Students More Chances to Think on Their Feet

Finally, interpersonal communication and live discussions should become even more important as the least corruptible formats of modern communication. Live, in-person interaction is one of the last places that AI cannot meaningfully affect. In a Socratic seminar, an oral defense, or a structured debate, students must think with what they actually have in their heads. When forced to respond impromptu to a challenge they did not script in advance, they get to practice real-time thinking. Even in my communication courses, where discussions, debates, and presentations are already central, I have added more low-stakes presentations, unrehearsed reflections, and on-the-spot “vibe checks” to encourage real-time cognitive practice.

The questions of what the future brings and how it impacts college graduates should be central for all universities and all our classrooms. Google captured its exhaust and built entire economy by recognizing that the byproduct was as valuable as the product itself. Universities now face similar choice where AI is the equivalent of the search engine and cognitive friction is our version the exhaust. Those institutions that learn to package and protect that friction at the same as they incorporate AI in educational system will produce graduates who are ready for the new era ahead of them. This approach does not demand entirely new pedagogical practices, but it does require rethinking of a few familiar habits. In the end, universities are expected to be slow to change but I hope more teachers commit to preserving cognitive friction with the same intentionality as they embrace AI.
